nameStory: This tiny hydroid gets its name from its distinctive trumpet-shaped feeding polyps that look like little elephant trunks - 'proboscis' means trunk or snout in Latin. The species name 'flavicirrata' refers to its yellowish tentacle-like structures, from 'flavus' meaning yellow and 'cirrus' meaning curl or tendril.
description: Proboscidactyla flavicirrata is a tiny colonial marine animal called a hydroid that looks like a delicate underwater plant. Each colony consists of numerous small polyps connected by thin stems, with the feeding polyps having a characteristic trumpet or funnel shape. The entire colony typically reaches only a few centimeters tall, making it easy to overlook among seaweed and other marine growth. Despite their plant-like appearance, these are actually simple animals related to jellyfish and sea anemones.

idTips.label: Trumpet-shaped polyps
idTips.description: The feeding polyps have a distinctive funnel or trumpet shape that flares outward, unlike the simple tube shape of most other hydroids

idTips.label: Yellowish coloration
idTips.description: Look for pale yellow to golden tints in the polyps and tentacles, especially visible under good lighting conditions

idTips.label: Delicate branching pattern
idTips.description: Colonies form sparse, irregular branches that feel soft and flexible when gently touched underwater

idTips.label: Small colony size
idTips.description: Entire colonies rarely exceed 3-4 centimeters in height, often growing as small tufts on rocks or shells

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Each polyp has a ring of fine, thread-like tentacles around the trumpet opening that wave gently in the current

habitat: This hydroid is found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, typically attached to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or pier pilings in the lower intertidal and subtidal zones. It prefers areas with good water circulation and is often discovered growing alongside other small marine organisms like barnacles and tube worms. Look for it in tide pools or while snorkeling in depths of just a few feet to about 30 feet.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin active growth as water temperatures warm, with new polyps appearing on existing stems. This is an excellent time to spot the characteristic trumpet shapes as they expand.
seasonality.summer: Peak growth period when colonies reach their largest size and are most easily identified. Polyps are fully extended and actively feeding during calm weather.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may still be visible but begin to slow their growth. Look for mature colonies with well-developed branching patterns before winter storms.
seasonality.winter: Many colonies die back or become dormant, though some may persist in sheltered locations. Identification becomes more challenging as polyps retract.

funFact: When disturbed, this hydroid can actually shoot tiny jellyfish-like creatures called medusae from special reproductive polyps - these microscopic 'babies' swim away to start new colonies elsewhere, making each hydroid colony a living jellyfish factory!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small hydroids like Obelia or Campanularia species, but those have bell-shaped rather than trumpet-shaped polyps. Remember: if it looks like a tiny trumpet or megaphone, you've likely found Proboscidactyla.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hydroids,' these animals are not plants at all but belong to the same group as jellyfish - the name comes from their superficial resemblance to plants when growing in colonies. Many people walk right past these fascinating creatures thinking they're looking at seaweed or algae.
compareHints: Since this is the only Proboscidactyla species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other small hydroids in the region. Unlike the cup-shaped polyps of Obelia species or the elongated tubes of Tubularia, Proboscidactyla's trumpet-shaped polyps are unique and diagnostic. The yellowish coloration also helps distinguish it from the typically colorless or whitish appearance of most other local hydroids.
